messages.content: My teacher said the test would be a piece of cake. Should I be worried?

No need to worry. "A piece of cake" means something very easy to do.
Example: After a week of practice, the long division sums were a piece of cake for Tanvi.
Accept vs except: I keep writing the wrong one in emails.

"Accept" is a verb that means to agree to take or receive something. "Except" means "but not" or "leaving out".
Examples: I accept your invitation. Everyone came to the meeting except Farhan.
What is the meaning of "carry on"?

"Carry on" means to continue doing something, often after a short stop.
Examples: The players carried on with the match after the rain stopped. Please carry on; I did not mean to interrupt.
How many c's and s's are there in "necessary"?

"Necessary" has one c and two s's. A memory trick: a shirt has one collar and two sleeves.
Example: Is it necessary to switch off the geyser after a bath?
Why would someone "spill the beans"? It sounds messy.

It is not about real beans. "Spill the beans" means to tell people something that was meant to be kept secret.
Example: Mira's little brother spilled the beans about the gift before her birthday.
Is it "taller then me" or "taller than me"?

It is "taller than me". Use "than" to compare two things. Use "then" for time, meaning "after that" or "at that moment".
Examples: Kabir runs faster than his coach. We warmed up, and then we started the race.
Could you explain "come across" in simple words?

"Come across" means to find or meet something by chance, without looking for it.
Example: While cleaning the shelf, Neel came across an old storybook with his grandfather's name inside.
Is it definately or definitely?

The correct spelling is "definitely". It comes from the word "finite", so remember the "finite" in the middle: de-finite-ly.
Example: I will definitely come to your housewarming on Sunday.
Can you tell me what "cost an arm and a leg" means?

It means to be very expensive.
Example: The leather jacket looked lovely, but it cost an arm and a leg, so Sofia bought a cotton one instead.
There, their, they're. Please help me sort these out!

"There" points to a place, or starts a sentence like "there is". "Their" means belonging to them. "They're" is short for "they are".
Example: They're leaving their bags over there by the gate.
What do people mean when they say they "ran out of" something?

"Run out of" means to use all of something so that none is left.
Examples: We ran out of milk, so Papa went to the shop. The printer has run out of ink.
Explain "beat around the bush" to me.

"Beat around the bush" means to avoid talking about the main point, usually because it is awkward.
Example: Stop beating around the bush, Vikram, and tell me if the project is late.
When do I use "your" and when "you're"?

"Your" shows that something belongs to you. "You're" is short for "you are". If you can say "you are" in the sentence, write "you're".
Example: You're welcome to borrow your cousin's cycle tomorrow.
I always misspell embarrass. Tips?

"Embarrass" has a double r and a double s. A memory trick: you go really red and smile shyly.
Example: Please do not embarrass me by singing in front of my friends.
Does "turn down" have more than one meaning?

Yes. "Turn down" can mean to lower the sound or heat. It can also mean to say no to an offer or request.
Examples: Please turn down the music; the baby is sleeping. Hana turned down the job because it was too far away.
To, too and two sound the same. How do I choose?

"Two" is the number 2. "Too" means "also" or "more than enough". "To" shows direction or comes before a verb, as in "to eat".
Example: I went to the canteen and ate two samosas, but they were too spicy.
"I'm going to hit the sack." What does this mean?

"Hit the sack" is an informal way of saying "go to bed".
Example: After the long train journey, Grace hit the sack at nine o'clock.
How do I use the phrasal verb "look up"?

"Look up" usually means to search for a piece of information, such as a word in a dictionary.
Examples: If you do not know a word, look it up. Dev looked up the train timings before leaving home.
Occassion, ocasion or occasion?

The correct spelling is "occasion": double c, single s.
Example: Diwali is a happy occasion when the whole family gets together.
A friend wrote "thanks for the complement". Is that spelled right?

No. It should be "compliment", which means kind words of praise. "Complement" means something that completes or goes well with another thing. Think: complement completes.
Examples: Thanks for the compliment. The green scarf complements her dress.
What does "in hot water" mean in English?

"In hot water" means in trouble, usually because you did something wrong.
Example: Zoya was in hot water with her parents after she came home two hours late.
Explain the different meanings of "pick up".

"Pick up" can mean to lift something, to collect someone in a vehicle, or to learn something without trying hard.
Examples: Pick up your shoes from the floor. Can you pick me up from the station? Kenji picked up some Tamil while living in Chennai.
Stationary or stationery: which one is pens and paper?

"Stationery" means pens, paper and envelopes. "Stationary" means not moving. A memory trick: stationery has an e for envelope.
Examples: Amara bought stationery for the new term. The bus was stationary at the signal.
Is tommorow spelled right?

Not quite. The correct spelling is "tomorrow": one m and two r's.
Example: The report is due tomorrow morning, so I will finish it tonight.
What does it mean when someone says "the ball is in your court"?

It means it is now your turn to decide or take the next step.
Example: I have said sorry to Riya twice, so the ball is in her court now.
"She was brought up by her grandparents." What does "bring up" mean here?

Here "bring up" means to look after a child until he or she is an adult. It can also mean to start talking about a subject.
Examples: Liam was brought up in a small town. Do not bring up exams at dinner tonight.
Desert and dessert look so alike. Which is the sweet dish?

"Dessert" is the sweet dish after a meal. "Desert" is a dry, sandy place. A memory trick: dessert has two s's because you always want a second helping.
Examples: We had kheer for dessert. Camels can walk across the desert for days.
How is "government" spelled? I always miss a letter.

It is spelled "government". Many people miss the n. Think of the verb "govern" and add "ment".
Example: The government opened a new library near our bus stop.
Meaning of "no use crying over spilt milk", please.

It means there is no point in being upset about something that has already happened and cannot be changed.
Example: The bus has already gone, and there is no use crying over spilt milk. Let us take an auto.
Do "get along with" and "get on with" mean the same?

Both can mean to have a friendly relationship with someone. "Get on with" is more common in British English, and it can also mean to continue doing a task.
Examples: Meera gets along with all her new colleagues. Stop chatting and get on with your work.
Breath vs breathe: which one is the verb?

"Breathe" is the verb, and it ends with an e. "Breath" is the noun, the air you take in or let out.
Examples: Breathe slowly when you feel nervous. Take a deep breath before you dive.
Is "enviroment" the correct spelling?

No. The correct spelling is "environment". There is an n before the m: environ-ment.
Example: Planting trees is one simple way to protect the environment.
What does "bite off more than you can chew" mean?

It means to try to do more than you are able to manage.
Example: Ravi took on three projects at once and soon realised he had bitten off more than he could chew.
My coach said the match was "called off". Will it happen later?

Probably not. "Call off" means to cancel something that was planned. If the match will happen later, people usually say it was "postponed".
Example: The match was called off because the ground was flooded.
I mix up quiet and quite. What's the difference?

"Quiet" means making little or no noise. "Quite" means "fairly" or "very". Quiet ends in -et, and quite ends with an e.
Example: The house was quiet after the guests left, and it felt quite empty.
Why is there an r after the b in February?

"February" comes from an old Latin word, and the r has always been part of it. Many people do not say the first r clearly, but you must write it: Feb-ru-ary.
Example: Our science exhibition is in February.
If I am "over the moon", how do I feel?

You feel extremely happy and pleased.
Example: Ishita was over the moon when she heard that her short story had won first prize.
What does "figure out" mean in this sentence: "I can't figure out this bill"?

"Figure out" means to understand something or find the answer after thinking about it. In your sentence, you cannot understand the bill.
Example: Omar finally figured out why the bill was so high: he had been charged twice for one item.
Do I lie down or lay down on the sofa?

You lie down. "Lie" means to rest flat, and it takes no object. "Lay" means to put something down, and it needs an object.
Examples: I will lie on the sofa for ten minutes. Please lay the plates on the table.
Wednesday is so hard to spell. Any trick?

Many people say it as "Wenz-day", but the spelling is "Wednesday". A trick is to say it the way it looks: Wed-nes-day.
Example: The team meeting moved from Tuesday to Wednesday.
My friend always "sits on the fence". What does that mean?

It means your friend avoids choosing a side in an argument or a decision.
Example: When we argued about where to eat, Kabir sat on the fence and said he was happy with anything.
Is "hand in" the same as "submit"?

Yes, mostly. "Hand in" means to give work or a document to a person in charge. It is less formal than "submit".
Example: Please hand in your project files by Friday.
What is the difference between rise and raise?

"Rise" means to go up by itself, so it has no object. "Raise" means to lift something or make it go up, so it needs an object.
Examples: The sun rises in the east. Raise your hand if you know the answer.
Calender or calendar?

The correct spelling is "calendar", ending in -ar. The word "calender" with -er is a rare machine word, so you almost never need it.
Example: Mummy marks all our birthdays on the kitchen calendar.
Our manager says "let's get on the same page". What does she mean?

She means she wants everyone to agree and understand the plan in the same way.
Example: Before the launch, the team met for ten minutes to make sure everyone was on the same page.
What is a "show-off"?

A show-off is a person who tries to make others admire what they have or can do. The verb is "show off".
Examples: Rohan kept showing off his new watch. Nobody enjoys sitting next to a show-off.
Bring or take: "Please ___ an umbrella when you go out."

Use "take". "Take" is for moving something away from where you are. "Bring" is for moving something towards where you are.
Examples: Take an umbrella when you go out. Bring your photos when you come to my house.
Is it "beleive" or "believe"?

It is "believe". The useful phrase is: never believe a lie. The word "lie" sits inside "believe".
Example: I believe you can do well in the interview.
What does "let's call it a day" mean?

It means to stop working on something for now, usually because you are tired or have done enough.
Example: By seven o'clock the shop was empty, so Mr Das decided to call it a day.
Meaning of "put up with"?

"Put up with" means to accept something unpleasant without complaining.
Example: People in our lane have to put up with loud horns all day.
Before exams my brother says he will "burn the midnight oil". Meaning?

It means to work or study until very late at night.
Example: Aditi burned the midnight oil all week to finish her history notes.
Should I say "she said me" or "she told me"?

Say "she told me". "Tell" is usually followed by the person: tell someone something. "Say" is followed by the words, or by "to" plus the person.
Examples: Nani told me a story. She said goodnight to everyone.
How would you use "come up with" in a sentence?

"Come up with" means to think of an idea, a plan or an answer.
Example: Sneha came up with a clever way to cut the waiting time at the front desk.
Rhythm has no vowels in the middle. How do I remember it?

Try this sentence: Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move. The first letters spell r-h-y-t-h-m.
Example: The tabla player kept a steady rhythm through the whole song.
What is "a blessing in disguise"?

It is something that seems bad at first but later turns out to be good.
Example: Missing the early train was a blessing in disguise, because Joseph met an old school friend on the next one.
Is there a difference between hear and listen?

Yes. You hear sounds without trying; it just happens. You listen when you pay attention on purpose. We say "listen to" something.
Examples: I heard a dog barking outside. Kwame likes to listen to old songs on the radio.
Our car "broke down" on the highway. Is that the right phrase?

Yes, it is right. "Break down" means that a machine or vehicle stops working. It can also mean to start crying suddenly.
Examples: Our car broke down near the toll gate. She broke down when she heard the sad news.
Restraunt or restaurant? I'm writing a review.

The correct spelling is "restaurant". Remember the "au" in the middle: rest-au-rant.
Example: The new South Indian restaurant near the station serves crisp dosas.
What does "get cold feet" mean? Is it about the weather?

No, it is not about the weather. "Get cold feet" means to suddenly feel too nervous to do something you planned.
Example: Faisal signed up for the singing contest, but he got cold feet the day before.
Do I "see" a cricket match on TV or "watch" it?

You watch it. "Watch" means to look at something for a while, usually something that moves or changes. "See" means to notice with your eyes, often without trying. "Look at" means to turn your eyes towards something on purpose.
Examples: We watched the final together. Look at that bird! I saw Bilal at the stadium.
"Let's catch up soon." What does my friend mean?

Your friend means "let us meet and talk about what has happened in our lives". "Catch up" can also mean to reach someone who is ahead of you.
Examples: Ayesha and I caught up over chai. Walk faster so we can catch up with the others.
How do I spell guarantee? The u confuses me.

It is spelled "guarantee". The u is silent, like in "guard" and "guess", and the word ends in double e.
Example: The mixer comes with a two-year guarantee.
Do we "make the dishes" or "do the dishes"?

We "do the dishes". In general, "do" goes with tasks and jobs, and "make" goes with creating something. Some phrases must simply be learned.
Examples: I do the dishes after dinner. Dad makes tea every morning. She did her homework and made her bed.
Can you explain "see eye to eye" with an example?

To "see eye to eye" means to agree with someone. It is often used in the negative.
Example: My sister and I do not see eye to eye on music, but we both love the same films.
What does "drop by" mean? My aunt said she would drop by.

It means she will make a short, informal visit, usually without a fixed plan.
Example: Gauri dropped by on her way home from work to return my umbrella.
People say "libary". What is the real spelling?

The real spelling is "library", with an r after the b. Say it slowly: li-brar-y.
Example: Tara borrowed three novels from the school library.
Are alone and lonely the same thing?

No. "Alone" means without other people. "Lonely" means sad because you have no company. You can be alone and still feel happy.
Examples: Pooja likes to read alone in her room. After moving to a new city, Ben felt lonely for a few weeks.
"You've hit the nail on the head." Is that praise?

Yes, it is praise. It means you have said exactly the right thing or found the real cause of a problem.
Example: When Karthik said the delays were caused by unclear instructions, he hit the nail on the head.
Explain "cut down on" please.

"Cut down on" means to do or use less of something.
Example: Mr Iyer is cutting down on sugar, so he now takes his coffee without it.
Is it maintainance or maintenance?

It is "maintenance". The verb is "maintain", but the noun drops the i: main-ten-ance.
Example: The lift in our building is closed for maintenance until noon.
Already or all ready: "We are ___ for the trip."

Write "all ready", which means completely prepared. "Already" is one word and means before now or sooner than expected.
Examples: We are all ready for the trip. The bus has already left.
My friend said he was "pulling my leg". What does that mean?

It means he was joking with you, usually by telling you something untrue in a playful way.
Example: When Liam said our teacher had cancelled exams forever, he was only pulling my leg.
When do people use "end up"?

People use "end up" when they reach a place or situation they did not plan, often after a series of events.
Example: We took a wrong turn and ended up at a beautiful lake.
Why is it pronunciation and not pronounciation?

The verb is "pronounce", but the noun drops the o: pro-nun-ci-a-tion. It is a common mistake, so check it twice.
Example: Our English teacher helps us with the pronunciation of difficult words.
"Altogether" and "all together": what is the difference?

"Altogether" means completely or in total. "All together" means everyone or everything in one place or at the same time.
Examples: The trip cost four thousand rupees altogether. The whole family sang all together at the wedding.
Is it rude to say "cut to the chase"?

It can sound a little impatient. It means to skip the extra details and talk about the most important thing.
Example: We only have five minutes, so let me cut to the chase: the client wants the design by Monday.
Find out: does it mean the same as discover?

Mostly, yes. "Find out" means to learn a fact or a piece of information, often by asking or checking. It is more common than "discover" in everyday speech.
Example: Shreya called the office to find out when the results would be announced.
Succesful, successfull or successful?

The correct spelling is "successful": double c, double s, and only one l at the end. The ending "-ful" always has one l.
Example: The charity run was successful and raised money for the shelter.
Beside and besides: is the s important?

Yes. "Beside" means next to. "Besides" means "also" or "apart from".
Examples: Put the lamp beside the bed. Besides cooking, Grandpa also enjoys gardening.
What does "go the extra mile" mean?

It means to make more effort than people expect from you.
Example: The nurse went the extra mile and stayed late to talk with the worried family.
Can "get over" be used for feelings?

Yes. "Get over" means to feel better after something unpleasant, like an illness, a shock or a sad event.
Example: It took Noor a few weeks to get over the loss of her pet cat.
How do you spell the word for a person you work with: colleage or colleague?

The correct spelling is "colleague", ending in -gue, like "league". Both words have the same "eague" pattern.
Example: My colleague Wei helped me fix the spreadsheet.
Between or among: "Divide the sweets ___ the five children."

Use "among" for a group where the members are not named one by one. Use "between" for two people or things, or for clearly separate items.
Examples: Divide the sweets among the five children. The secret stayed between Sara and me.
I heard "I missed the boat" at a sale. Explain?

"Miss the boat" means to lose a chance because you were too slow to act.
Example: The sale ended yesterday, so I missed the boat on those cheap cushions.
Is "hang out" formal English?

No, it is informal. "Hang out" means to spend relaxed time somewhere, often with friends.
Examples: On Saturdays we hang out at the park near Simran's house. Where do you usually hang out after college?
Shedule or schedule?

The correct spelling is "schedule", with sch at the start. In British English it is often said "shed-yool", and in American English "sked-yool".
Example: Please check the schedule before you book the meeting room.
Do people still use "whom"?

Yes, mostly in formal writing. Use "who" for the person doing the action and "whom" for the person receiving it, often after a preposition. In everyday speech, "who" is fine.
Examples: Who wrote this book? To whom should I send the letter?
What does "a drop in the ocean" mean?

It means an amount that is very small compared to what is needed.
Example: Cleaning one beach was only a drop in the ocean, but the volunteers felt it was a good start.
When someone says "hold on", what should I do?

You should wait for a short time. "Hold on" can also mean to hold something tightly.
Examples: Hold on, I will get my keys. Hold on to the rail when the train starts.
How many m's are in "recommend"?

"Recommend" has one c and two m's. Think of it as "re" plus "commend".
Example: Can you recommend a good mystery novel for the holidays?
Who's or whose: "___ bag is this?"

Write "Whose". "Whose" asks who something belongs to. "Who's" is short for "who is" or "who has".
Examples: Whose bag is this? Who's coming to the science fair?
What does "face the music" mean?

It means to accept the bad results of something you have done.
Example: Lin forgot to do her homework, so she had to face the music in class.
How is "keep up with" used?

"Keep up with" means to move or work at the same speed as someone or something, so you do not fall behind.
Examples: Dev cycles fast, and I can hardly keep up with him. It is hard to keep up with all the news.
Is "neighbor" wrong? My book says "neighbour".

Neither is wrong. "Neighbour" is British spelling, used in India. "Neighbor" is American spelling. Choose one and use it consistently.
Example: Our neighbour waters our plants when we go away.
Everyday or every day: "I walk ___."

Write "every day", two words, which means each day. "Everyday" is one word and is an adjective meaning ordinary or normal, used before a noun.
Examples: I walk every day. Walking is an easy everyday habit.
What does "get the ball rolling" mean?

It means to start an activity or a process.
Example: To get the ball rolling for the Pongal celebration, Anjali made a list of who would bring what.
What does "let someone down" mean?

It means to disappoint someone by not doing what they hoped or expected.
Example: Ravi promised to help with the move, and he did not let us down.
Is it temprature or temperature?

It is "temperature". Many people miss the e after the p. Say it slowly: tem-per-a-ture.
Example: The temperature dropped sharply after the evening rain.
Maybe or may be: "It ___ the best Holi ever!"

Write "may be", two words, because it is a verb phrase meaning "might be". "Maybe" is one word and means "perhaps".
Examples: It may be the best Holi ever! Maybe we will play with colours in the morning.
We all "chipped in" for the farewell gift. Is that correct English?

Yes, it is correct and informal. "Chip in" means to give a share of money or help so that a group can do something together. It can also mean to add a comment in a conversation.
Examples: Ten of us chipped in for the gift. Elena chipped in with a useful idea.
My coach told me to "keep my chin up" after we lost. What did he mean?

He meant you should stay cheerful and hopeful even though things are difficult right now.
Example: Keep your chin up, Raghav; one bad match does not make you a bad player.
Emigrate or immigrate: which one is leaving a country?

"Emigrate" means to leave your own country to live in another one. "Immigrate" means to come into a new country to live there. Remember: emigrate is exit, immigrate is in.
Examples: Mateo's family emigrated from Spain. They immigrated to Canada in 2015.
What does "go over" mean when a teacher says "let's go over the answers"?

It means to look at or check something carefully, often again, from start to end.
Example: Before the exam, Nikita went over her notes one last time.
Buisness or business? I can never remember.

The correct spelling is "business". Think of it as "busy" plus "ness": the y changes to i, giving bus-i-ness.
Example: Harpreet's uncle runs a small business selling handmade candles.
Someone told me to "break a leg" before my concert. Was that rude?

Not at all. "Break a leg" is a friendly way to wish a performer good luck before a show.
Example: Before Ira went on stage to sing, her friends whispered, "Break a leg!"
Farther or further: which one is correct for distance?

Both are used for distance, but "farther" is only for physical distance. "Further" can also mean more or extra, as in further details.
Examples: The temple is farther than it looks. Please write to us for further information.
"Make up" seems to have many meanings. What are the main ones?

The main meanings are: to become friends again after a quarrel, to invent a story or excuse, and to form a whole.
Examples: Tom and Ayesha argued, but they made up the next day. Do not make up excuses. Girls make up half of our class.
How many d's does "address" have?

"Address" has two d's and two s's: a-dd-re-ss.
Example: Please write your full address on the form, including the pin code.
What does "we are all in the same boat" mean?

It means everyone is in the same difficult situation.
Example: Nobody understood the new maths chapter, so the whole class was in the same boat.
Imply and infer: who does what?

The speaker or writer implies, which means suggests something without saying it directly. The listener or reader infers, which means works it out from clues.
Examples: The letter implied that the uncle was angry. From the last chapter, I inferred that the twins would meet again.
Why do people say "passed away" instead of "died"?

"Pass away" means to die. People use it because it sounds gentler and kinder, especially when talking to someone who is grieving.
Example: Grace's grandfather passed away last spring, and the family still remembers him with love.
Is committee spelled with double letters?

Yes, three sets of them: double m, double t and double e. Write it as co-mm-i-tt-ee.
Example: The festival committee met to plan the decorations.
Explain "wear your heart on your sleeve".

It means to show your feelings openly, so that others can easily see them.
Example: Dev wears his heart on his sleeve; you always know when he is happy or upset.
Practice or practise: is one of them American?

In British and Indian English, "practice" is the noun and "practise" is the verb. American English uses "practice" for both.
Examples: Sitar practice starts at six. I practise the sitar every evening.
What does "point out" mean?

"Point out" means to tell someone about something they may not have noticed.
Example: Lucas pointed out a small spelling mistake in the poster before it was printed.
Is it mischievious or mischievous?

It is "mischievous", with only three syllables: mis-chie-vous. There is no extra i before the ending.
Example: My mischievous little brother hid all the TV remotes.
My sister said I would clean my room "when pigs fly". Meaning?

She means she thinks it will never happen. It is a joking way of saying something is impossible.
Example: "Rohan will wake up early on a holiday when pigs fly," laughed his mother.
Driving licence or driving license: which is correct in India?

In British and Indian English, "licence" with a c is the noun, and "license" with an s is the verb. So write "driving licence". American English uses "license" for both.
Example: Simran got her driving licence last month.
"I ran into Meena at the market." Did I hit her?

No. Here "run into" means to meet someone by chance. It can also mean to have a problem, or to crash into something.
Examples: I ran into Meena at the market. We ran into trouble with the booking.
Privilege keeps getting a red line under it. I keep adding a d.

There is no d. The correct spelling is "privilege": two i's at the start and "lege" at the end, like "legend" without the "nd".
Example: It was a privilege to meet the author at our school.
What does "time to hit the road" mean?

It means it is time to leave or start a journey.
Example: We packed the snacks at dawn and hit the road before the traffic started.
Council and counsel: which one is a group of people?

A "council" is a group of people chosen to make decisions, such as a city council. "Counsel" means advice, or to give advice, and in law it can mean a lawyer.
Examples: The council voted to repair the old park. She asked her teacher for counsel.
What does "set off" mean in a travel plan?

"Set off" means to start a journey. It can also mean to cause something to start, such as an alarm.
Examples: We set off for Ooty at five in the morning. The smoke from the toast set off the alarm.
Acheive or achieve?

The correct spelling is "achieve". Use the "i before e" rule: there is no c just before it, so it is i then e.
Example: Hard training helped Kwame achieve his best time in the race.
An old friend called me "out of the blue". What does that mean?

It means something happened suddenly and unexpectedly.
Example: Out of the blue, Ifeoma got a letter from her pen friend after ten years.
Discreet and discrete sound the same. Do they mean the same?

No. "Discreet" means careful not to embarrass people or share private things. "Discrete" means separate and distinct.
Examples: Please be discreet about the surprise party. The course is divided into five discrete units.
My mother keeps talking about me "settling down". What is that?

"Settle down" can mean to start a calmer life in one place, often with a steady job or family. It can also mean to become calm and quiet.
Examples: Sanjay wants to travel before he settles down. The children settled down after the story began.
Arguement or argument?

The correct spelling is "argument". The verb "argue" loses its final e before "ment".
Example: Bilal and Omar had a small argument about the score, but they soon laughed about it.
Explain "the tip of the iceberg".

It means a small, visible part of a much bigger problem or situation. Most of an iceberg lies under the water.
Example: The plastic on the beach was only the tip of the iceberg; much more lay under the sea.
Historic or historical novel?

Say "historical novel". "Historical" means connected with the past. "Historic" means important in history.
Examples: Elena loves historical novels set in old Delhi. The moon landing was a historic event.
Is "show up" the same as "arrive"?

Yes, in informal English. "Show up" means to arrive or appear, often when people are expecting you, or sometimes not expecting you.
Example: Fifty people showed up for the Lohri bonfire, much more than we had planned for.
How many s's and p's are in disappoint?

"Disappoint" has one s and two p's. Think of "dis" plus "appoint".
Example: Do not let one bad day disappoint you too much.
What does "add fuel to the fire" mean?

It means to make an angry situation or argument worse.
Example: My parents were already upset, and my cheeky reply only added fuel to the fire.
Economic or economical: "This scooter is very ___ to run."

Write "economical". "Economical" means not costing much or not wasting money. "Economic" is about the economy, trade and industry of a country.
Examples: This scooter is very economical to run. The news report was about economic growth.
What does "sort out" mean?

"Sort out" means to arrange things neatly or to solve a problem.
Examples: Neel sorted out his old books and gave some to his cousin. Let us sort out this misunderstanding calmly.
Independant or independent?

The correct spelling is "independent", with -ent at the end. All three vowels after the d are e's: in-de-pen-dent.
Example: After she moved to Pune, Shreya became more independent.
Meaning of "won by the skin of their teeth"?

It means they won, but only just, with almost no margin.
Example: The team won the final by the skin of their teeth, with one run to spare.
Sensible and sensitive: what is the difference?

"Sensible" means showing good judgement and common sense. "Sensitive" means easily affected by feelings or by things like light or heat.
Examples: Wearing a raincoat was a sensible choice. Anika is sensitive and notices when a friend is sad.
"You take after your father." What does it mean?

It means you look or behave like an older member of your family, here your father.
Example: Tara takes after her grandmother; they both love painting and laugh in the same way.
Is there a d in knowledge?

Yes. "Knowledge" is spelled k-n-o-w-l-e-d-g-e. It starts with a silent k and has "dge" near the end, like "edge".
Example: Reading widely gives you knowledge about many places and people.
What does "every cloud has a silver lining" mean?

It means that even a bad situation usually has some good side to it.
Example: Rest at home after the injury was boring, but every cloud has a silver lining: Mira finished three novels.
Personal or personnel department?

Say "personnel department". "Personnel" means the people who work for an organisation. "Personal" means belonging to one person or private.
Examples: The personnel department handles new staff. Please do not read my personal diary.
"I want to take up yoga." Is that correct?

Yes, it is correct. "Take up" means to start a new hobby or activity. It can also mean to fill space or time.
Examples: Kenji took up badminton last winter. This sofa takes up half the room.
Foriegn or foreign?

The correct spelling is "foreign". It breaks the "i before e" rule, so you need to remember it: for-eign.
Example: Diego enjoys learning about foreign foods and festivals.
Can you explain "actions speak louder than words"?

It means what people do shows their true feelings better than what they say.
Example: Karan says he is a good friend, but actions speak louder than words, and he always helps when it matters.
Is "cloth" the singular of "clothes"?

No. "Cloth" is material, like cotton or silk. "Clothes" are things you wear, and the word has no singular form. For one item, say "a piece of clothing".
Examples: Nani bought two metres of cloth. I packed my clothes for the trip.
Does adding "away" change the meaning of "throw"?

Yes. "Throw" means to send something through the air. "Throw away" means to get rid of something you do not want.
Examples: Throw the ball to Liam. Do not throw away plastic bottles; put them in the recycling bin.
Is weird spelled wierd?

No. It is "weird": w-e-i-r-d. It is an exception to the "i before e" rule.
Example: We heard a weird noise from the kitchen, but it was only the cat.
Custom and costume: what is the difference?

A "custom" is a usual way of doing things in a place or group. A "costume" is a set of clothes worn to look like someone else, such as at a play.
Example: It is our custom to wear new clothes at Eid, but at the school play, Noor wore a lion costume.
In a shop, do I "try" a shirt or "try on" a shirt?

You try on a shirt. "Try" means to attempt something or to taste or test it. "Try on" means to put on clothes or shoes to see if they fit.
Examples: Try this new pickle. Sara tried on three pairs of sandals before buying one.
"That was the last straw!" my dad shouted. What does it mean?

It means the final problem in a series of problems, the one that makes someone lose patience completely.
Example: The tap had leaked for weeks, and when the ceiling started dripping too, it was the last straw.
Peace or piece: "Can I have a ___ of cake?"

Write "piece", which means a part of something. "Peace" means calm or no fighting. A memory trick: a piece of pie.
Examples: Can I have a piece of cake? After the guests left, there was peace in the house.
Telling an upset friend to "calm down": rude or fine?

"Calm down" means to become less upset or excited. Saying it directly to an upset person can sound rude, so it is kinder to use it about "us" or about others.
Examples: Let us sit for a minute until we both calm down. The baby calmed down after his feed.
Is "alot" one word?

No. "A lot" is always two words. "Alot" is not a correct spelling.
Example: Yusuf puts a lot of ginger in his chai.
What does "back to square one" mean?

It means to go back to the very start of something because your attempt did not work.
Example: The storm blew away all our seedlings, so we were back to square one in the garden.
Can you explain weak and week? They sound the same.

Yes, they sound the same. "Week" means seven days. "Weak" means not strong.
Example: After a week of fever, Esther felt weak, so she rested at home.
What do "check in" and "check out" mean at a hotel?

To "check in" means to arrive and register at a hotel or airport. To "check out" means to pay and leave a hotel.
Examples: We checked in at the hotel at noon. Guests must check out by eleven in the morning.
Alright or all right?

"All right" is the standard spelling and is always safe in formal writing. "Alright" is common in informal writing, but some teachers mark it wrong.
Example: Are you all right after that fall?
What does "like a fish out of water" mean?

It means feeling uncomfortable because you are in a place or situation that is new or strange to you.
Example: On his first day in the big city, Aditya felt like a fish out of water.
Plain and plane: which one flies?

"Plane" is the one that flies; it is short for aeroplane. "Plain" means simple, or a wide, flat area of land.
Examples: The plane landed in Kochi on time. Fatima wore a plain white kurta.
What does "you can count on me" mean?

It means you can trust me and depend on me to help you.
Example: Whenever there is a family function, we can count on Chachi to arrange the food.
Is "could of" correct? I see it a lot online.

No, it is a mistake. The correct form is "could have". In speech, "could've" sounds like "could of", which causes the confusion. The same is true for "should have" and "would have".
Example: I could have finished the novel last night, but I fell asleep.
What does "having butterflies in your stomach" mean?

It means feeling nervous, usually before something important.
Example: Riya had butterflies in her stomach before her first veena recital.
Brake or break: "Press the ___ at the red light."

Write "brake", the part of a vehicle that slows it down. "Break" means to damage something into pieces, or a short rest.
Examples: Press the brake at the red light. We took a short break after an hour of walking.
No onions at home. Can I say we will "do without" them?

Yes, that is a good use. "Do without" means to manage even though you do not have something.
Example: We had no onions, so we had to do without them in the curry.
Colour or color: which spelling is right?

Both are right. "Colour" is British spelling, used in India. "Color" is American spelling. Just use one style in the same piece of writing.
Example: The leaves change colour in autumn.
What does "learn the ropes" mean?

It means to learn the basic skills of a new job or activity.
Example: It took Mateo a month to learn the ropes at the swimming club.
Story or storey for floors of a building?

In British and Indian English, a "storey" is a floor of a building, and a "story" is a tale. American English uses "story" for both.
Examples: We live in a three-storey building. Nana told us a story about his village.
Explain "get by" with an example.

"Get by" means to manage to live or do something with difficulty, using what you have.
Examples: As a student, Jonah got by on a small monthly allowance. Hana gets by in French, but she is not fluent.
Travelling or traveling?

"Travelling" with two l's is British spelling, used in India. American English uses "traveling" with one l. The same is true for "cancelled" and "canceled".
Example: Wei is travelling to Shimla next week.
Can you explain the idiom "a storm in a teacup"?

It means a lot of anger or worry about something that is not really important.
Example: The fight over who got the window seat was a storm in a teacup; the cousins were laughing ten minutes later.
Cereal or serial: which one is breakfast?

"Cereal" is a grain such as wheat, rice or oats, or a breakfast food made from it. "Serial" means in a series, like a story told in parts on TV.
Examples: Nisha eats cereal with milk. Grandma watches a TV serial every evening.
What does "give away" mean?

"Give away" means to give something for free. It can also mean to tell a secret by accident.
Examples: During the festival, the temple gives away free sweets. Her smile gave away the surprise.
Cieling or ceiling?

The correct spelling is "ceiling". It follows the rule "i before e, except after c": c-e-i.
Example: Papa painted the ceiling a soft cream colour.
What does "turn over a new leaf" mean?

It means to change your behaviour and start acting in a better way.
Example: Sanjay turned over a new leaf and now goes for a walk every morning instead of sleeping late.
Do I say "I am boring" or "I am bored"?

Say "I am bored". The -ed form describes how you feel. The -ing form describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Examples: I am bored because it is raining. This long train journey is boring.
Can milk "go off"?

Yes. When food goes off, it becomes bad and is not safe to eat. "Go off" can also mean that an alarm rings or that a light stops working.
Examples: The milk went off in the heat. My alarm went off at six.
Is it hieght, heighth or height?

The correct spelling is "height". It has no h at the end, unlike "width" and "length".
Example: The basketball coach checked the height of each player.
What does "take it with a pinch of salt" mean?

It means not to believe something completely, because it may not be true.
Example: The book claims the castle had a hundred rooms, but I take that with a pinch of salt.
Ago or before: "I visited Goa two years ___."

Write "ago". "Ago" counts back from now and comes after the length of time. "Before" means earlier than another time or event.
Examples: I visited Goa two years ago. Please reach the station before ten.
Is it "look forward to meet you" or "look forward to meeting you"?

It is "look forward to meeting you". In this phrase, "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing verb.
Examples: I look forward to meeting you. The children look forward to Christmas all year.
Grammer or grammar?

The correct spelling is "grammar", ending in -ar. Notice the two a's: gr-a-mm-a-r. There is no e anywhere in the word.
Example: This little book explains English grammar in simple steps.
Why would someone say "hold your horses" at dinner?

They are asking you to wait and not rush. It is a light, friendly way to say "slow down".
Example: Hold your horses, Kabir; the rice is still cooking.
During or while: "I fell asleep ___ the concert."

Write "during". "During" is followed by a noun. "While" is followed by a subject and verb.
Examples: I fell asleep during the concert. I fell asleep while the band was playing.
What does "tidy up" mean?

"Tidy up" means to make a place neat by putting things where they belong.
Example: Before the guests arrived, Deepa and her brother tidied up the living room.
Excercise or exercise?

The correct spelling is "exercise". There is no c after the x: ex-er-cise.
Example: Nani does gentle exercise, like a short walk after dinner.
Grandpa calls my sister "the apple of his eye". Meaning?

It means she is a person he loves very much and is very proud of.
Example: Little Anika is the apple of her grandfather's eye.
Elder or older: "My ___ brother is a doctor."

Both are correct here, before a noun about family. "Elder" is used only for people, mostly family, and never with "than". "Older" can be used for anything and with "than".
Examples: My elder brother is a doctor. He is older than me by four years.
What does "brush up on" mean?

"Brush up on" means to practise and improve a skill or knowledge that you have partly forgotten.
Example: Before her trip to Paris, Elena brushed up on her French.
How can a word like queue have so many vowels?

"Queue" comes from French. It sounds just like the letter q, but you write q and then u-e twice: q-u-e-u-e.
Example: There was a long queue at the bakery on Sunday morning.
What is "a white elephant"?

It is something that costs a lot of money to keep but is not useful.
Example: The huge fountain in the town square became a white elephant; it never had water.
Remember or remind: "Please ___ me to buy milk."

Write "remind". To "remind" means to help someone else remember. To "remember" means to keep something in your own mind.
Examples: Please remind me to buy milk. I remembered my keys this time.
What does "stand out" mean?

"Stand out" means to be easy to see or notice because something is different or better.
Example: Among all the singers, Tara's clear voice really stood out.
Vegtable or vegetable?

The correct spelling is "vegetable", with an e after the g: veg-e-ta-ble. People often drop it when they speak quickly.
Example: Our favourite vegetable is lady's finger fried with a little spice.
Meaning of "she stole the show"?

It means she got the most attention and praise at an event, usually because she was so good.
Example: At the Navratri dance, eight-year-old Mira stole the show with her quick steps.
Rob or steal: "Someone ___ my bike."

Write "stole". You steal a thing. You rob a person or a place, such as a bank.
Examples: Someone stole my bike from outside the gym. The shop was robbed last night.
Grow or grow up: can plants grow up?

No, plants just grow. "Grow" means to get bigger, and it is used for people, plants and animals. "Grow up" is only for people, and means to become an adult.
Examples: These tomatoes grow fast in the sun. Kwame grew up in a village near the hills.
Did we "win" the other team or "beat" them?

You beat them. You win a game, a match or a prize. You beat a person or a team.
Examples: We won the final. We beat the other team by two goals.
Put on or wear: "I ___ a jacket because it was cold."

Write "put on". "Put on" is the action of getting dressed in something. "Wear" means to have it on your body.
Examples: I put on a jacket because it was cold. Simran wears glasses for reading.
Is Holi "fun" or "funny"?

Holi is fun. "Fun" means enjoyable. "Funny" means it makes you laugh.
Examples: Playing with colours is fun. My uncle covered in green powder looked really funny.
